interviewQuestions.question: Explain temporal and spatial locality, and how a CPU cache exploits each.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Temporal locality is reuse of the *same* address soon after it was last touched — a loop counter incremented every iteration, a hot function's local variables. Caches exploit this simply by keeping recently-used data resident: as long as the line hasn't been evicted, the next access to that same address hits instead of paying RAM latency again.

Spatial locality is accessing addresses *near* one another in a short window — walking an array, reading consecutive struct fields, executing sequential instructions. Caches exploit this by fetching an entire block (typically 64 bytes) on any miss rather than just the requested word, so the unrequested neighbors arrive for free and are very likely to be touched next.

A concrete trace: summing a large `int` array in a loop hits temporal locality on the loop index and accumulator (same registers/cache line touched every iteration) and spatial locality on the array elements (each 64-byte line fetch delivers 16 ints at once, so only every 16th access is a genuine miss). Break either assumption — say, indexing the array with a stride larger than the line size, or accessing a working set that never gets touched twice — and the hit rate collapses toward the RAM-limited case regardless of how big the cache is.

**Testing:** whether you name both forms precisely and map each to the specific mechanism that exploits it, rather than saying "caches use locality" without connecting cause to effect.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Temporal vs spatial locality

interviewQuestions.question: A teammate says a slow program just needs more RAM. When is that wrong?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd separate *capacity* from *locality* before agreeing. More RAM only helps a genuine capacity problem — the program is swapping to disk, or its working set literally doesn't fit in physical memory, so pages are getting evicted and refetched. If that's the symptom (high page-fault rate, swap activity), more RAM is the right fix.

But if the working set fits comfortably in the RAM already installed and the program is still slow, the bottleneck is almost always locality, not capacity — a cache-unfriendly access pattern like column-major traversal of a large row-major matrix, or randomly indexing into a huge structure with no reuse. In that case every access jumps to a new cache line, evicting a line that was just fetched (and mostly unused) before its neighbors could be reused. Adding RAM does nothing here: the data was never the problem, the *access order* through a fixed-size, fast cache was — and no amount of slow DRAM capacity fixes a cache-hierarchy bottleneck sitting between the CPU and that RAM.

The fix for a locality problem is algorithmic: reorder loops for sequential access, tile the working set into cache-sized chunks, restructure data layout so hot fields are contiguous. I'd confirm which problem it actually is with cache-miss and page-fault counters (`perf stat` on Linux shows both) before proposing either fix — guessing wastes a hardware purchase on a software problem, or vice versa.

**Testing:** whether you distinguish a capacity bottleneck from a locality bottleneck with a concrete diagnostic, instead of reaching for "buy more hardware."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: RAM vs locality

interviewQuestions.question: Why does the memory hierarchy have several distinct levels instead of one size tuned to be "good enough"?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because size and latency are in direct physical tension, and there's no single size that's both fast enough and large enough for what programs actually need. A larger storage array needs longer wires and more circuitry to search, which mechanically increases access latency — you can't make an SRAM array both big and one-cycle-fast at the same time, and DRAM trades that latency for vastly higher density but pays hundreds of cycles of latency and needs an entirely different, off-chip technology.

So the hierarchy stacks several technologies, each sized to be as fast as the tier above needs while being as large as the tier below can afford to be slow: registers (a handful of words, sub-cycle), L1 (tens of KB, 1-4 cycles), L2 (hundreds of KB to a few MB, ~10 cycles), L3 (tens of MB shared across cores, ~30-50 cycles), DRAM (tens to hundreds of GB, ~100-300 cycles), and disk/SSD (TBs, microseconds to milliseconds). Each level exists because the level above is too small for the working set and the level below is too slow to access directly on every reference — locality is what makes this work at all: if programs accessed memory uniformly at random, a small fast cache would provide no benefit regardless of how well-tuned it was, since every access would still need to reach the big slow level most of the time.

The reason this is durable across decades of chip design rather than a temporary compromise: the gap between CPU cycle time and DRAM latency has grown, not shrunk, over generations (the "memory wall"), so more levels of hierarchy — not fewer — have kept being added (L3 was uncommon decades ago, now nearly universal) to keep bridging that widening gap.

**Testing:** whether you connect hierarchy depth to a genuine physical constraint (size-latency trade-off) and to the memory wall trend, not just describe the levels.
